misconceptions.statement: Only educated people or people who own property can vote.
misconceptions.why: Old rules in many countries and some village talk linked voting to schooling or land.
misconceptions.fix: Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above can vote, whether rich or poor, educated or not, man or woman, of any caste or religion.

probe.question: Ramesh is 40, cannot read, and owns no land. Can he vote in the Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because he is not educated and owns no property.

misconceptions.statement: Election officials can see which candidate each person voted for.
misconceptions.why: Students see officials handling the machine and the voter list and assume they can link a name to a vote.
misconceptions.fix: The voter list and the EVM votes are kept separate. Votes are counted only in total for each candidate, so no one can tell how any one person voted.

probe.question: After you vote, can the polling officer find out whom you voted for?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the officer can check the machine and see my choice.

misconceptions.root_belief: Officials can link voters to their votes
misconceptions.source_hint: Election Commission of India voter education material

misconceptions.statement: EVMs are connected to the internet or Wi-Fi, so they can be hacked from far away.
misconceptions.why: Students think all digital devices are online, and social media rumours repeat this.
misconceptions.fix: Indian EVMs are standalone machines. They have no internet, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, and run a one-time programmed chip, so they cannot be controlled remotely.

probe.question: How is an EVM connected to the counting centre during voting?
probe.wrong_answer: It is connected through the internet and sends the votes online.

misconceptions.root_belief: Every electronic device is networked online
misconceptions.source_hint: Election Commission of India EVM FAQs

misconceptions.statement: The EVM is one single unit where the voter presses a button and the vote is counted inside the same box.
misconceptions.why: Students picture a simple machine with buttons and miss that there are two parts.
misconceptions.fix: The EVM has a Ballot Unit, where the voter presses the button, and a Control Unit, which stays with the polling officer and records the votes. A cable joins them.

probe.question: How many main parts does an EVM have and which one does the voter use?
probe.wrong_answer: One part only, and the voter uses it as well as the officer.

misconceptions.root_belief: EVM is a single undivided device

misconceptions.statement: The VVPAT slip is given to the voter to take home as proof of the vote.
misconceptions.why: Students think a printed slip is like a receipt and should be carried away.
misconceptions.fix: The voter sees the slip through a glass window for about 7 seconds. It then drops into a sealed box and is not handed over, which also keeps the vote secret.

probe.question: What happens to the VVPAT slip after you see it?
probe.wrong_answer: I take it home with me as a receipt.

misconceptions.root_belief: A printed slip is a receipt to keep
misconceptions.source_hint: Election Commission of India VVPAT guidelines

misconceptions.statement: A NOTA vote is a wasted or invalid vote, like leaving the ballot blank.
misconceptions.why: Students think that voting for none of the candidates means the vote is not counted.
misconceptions.fix: NOTA is an option on the EVM and a NOTA vote is a valid vote that is counted and recorded. It lets a voter say they reject all candidates.

probe.question: If 500 people press NOTA, are those votes counted as valid votes?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are wasted votes and not counted.

misconceptions.root_belief: Rejecting all candidates makes a vote invalid

misconceptions.statement: If NOTA gets the most votes, the election is cancelled and held again.
misconceptions.why: Students think the largest share of votes always decides the outcome, even if it is NOTA.
misconceptions.fix: Even if NOTA gets the most votes, the candidate with the most votes among the actual candidates is declared the winner. NOTA does not cause a re-election.

probe.question: In a seat NOTA gets 5,000 votes and the best candidate gets 4,000. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: NOTA wins so the election is cancelled and held again.

misconceptions.root_belief: NOTA has power to cancel elections
misconceptions.source_hint: ECI clarification on NOTA; news explainers

misconceptions.statement: The Election Commission is part of the ruling government and takes orders from the Prime Minister.
misconceptions.why: Students see ministers and officials together and assume the commission works under the government of the day.
misconceptions.fix: The Election Commission is an independent constitutional body under Article 324. It conducts elections without taking orders from the government.

probe.question: Who controls the Election Commission's decisions during elections?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister and the ruling party control it.

misconceptions.root_belief: All official bodies work under the government

misconceptions.statement: The Model Code of Conduct applies only on the polling day.
misconceptions.why: Students link elections only to the day of voting and miss the campaign period.
misconceptions.fix: The Model Code of Conduct starts when the Election Commission announces the election schedule and stays in force until the results are declared.

probe.question: For how long does the Model Code of Conduct apply?
probe.wrong_answer: Only on the day people vote.

misconceptions.root_belief: Election rules apply only on voting day
misconceptions.source_hint: Election Commission of India MCC manual

misconceptions.statement: The Model Code of Conduct is a law and breaking it sends a candidate straight to jail.
misconceptions.why: Students treat any official rule for elections as a criminal law with fixed punishments.
misconceptions.fix: The Model Code is a set of guidelines agreed by parties, not a separate law. Its aim is to stop ruling parties from misusing government power, such as announcing new schemes or using official vehicles for campaigns. The Commission can warn or censure, and some acts also break other laws.

probe.question: Can a minister use a government vehicle for campaigning during the code period?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a minister can use it freely because they are in government.

misconceptions.root_belief: Rules are either full law or no rule

misconceptions.statement: A candidate must get more than half of all votes to win a seat.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the idea of a majority from class votes and think winning needs 50 percent.
misconceptions.fix: In Indian Lok Sabha and Assembly elections, the candidate who gets the most votes wins, even with less than half of the total. This is called first past the post.

probe.question: Four candidates get 30%, 28%, 22% and 20% of the votes. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: Nobody wins because no one has more than 50 percent.

misconceptions.root_belief: Winning always needs an absolute majority

misconceptions.statement: Voters directly vote for the Prime Minister on the EVM.
misconceptions.why: Media talk about leaders and party faces makes students think the PM's name appears on the ballot.
misconceptions.fix: Voters choose a candidate for their own constituency to be MP. The party or alliance with a majority of MPs chooses the Prime Minister.

probe.question: Whose name do you find on the EVM in a Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: The name of the Prime Minister candidate.

misconceptions.root_belief: People directly elect the head of government

misconceptions.statement: Voting is compulsory in India and a person who does not vote is punished.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that voting is a duty and assume it is legally required, like attending school.
misconceptions.fix: Voting is a right and an important duty, but it is not compulsory in India and there is no punishment for not voting.

probe.question: What happens to a citizen who does not vote in India?
probe.wrong_answer: They are fined or punished by the government.
